title: About use cases of AI
author: YesterdayOptimal3552
selftext:
Very new to Reddit, but I want to ask something...

Want to know what your balance is in your workflow between traditional ways and generative AI ways.

Current AI still seems clumsy to me; when I want to make something precisely, it becomes a nightmare to shape exactly as I imagine, which makes me think AI is hardly different from other tools.

Sometimes it seems easier not to use AI…  
If I can imagine clearly what I want to draw/write/compose and how to do it, then it will be faster to make it myself than to elaborate/give context to AI.  
If I have one sample asset that suits your project and I only need a similar art direction, then I can let AI make the rest.

Of course, there are more indirect/combinated use cases: I can let AI make some tools specialized to my project (e.g., for an RPG, an enemy data manager that exports in a specific JSON format).

Perhaps I am using AI very poorly…  
What do you think about this kind of balance in the workflow?

comments.author: 3tt07kjt
comments.body:
My balance is traditional methods for art / writing / music / game design, and heavy use of AI for code and tools.

YMMV. I have a programming background, so I can get a lot of mileage out of making AI do coding for me.

comments.author: josh_the_dev
comments.body:
For me personally I think it's really cool to use in prototyping due to the speed. I don't need to know how something works internally if I'm not using it much further anyway.

I also use AI often to build small tools. Again the speed makes it viable here. If the investment is super small much more of these small improvements are actually worth it.

Other than that I use AI to get higher quality output that I would be able to get myself. E.g. using video to animation allows me to get good base for character animations that only needs some cleanup. Technical stuff like the cleanup I can do but I am just not a good animator

replies.author: YesterdayOptimal3552
replies.body:
sounds good  
I still don't get used to quick prototyping, for I feel my goal is getting heavily influenced and biased by outcomes from my short incomplete prompt...

replies.author: josh_the_dev
replies.body:
Thats fine, you should get influenced by your prototype. If it's fun or you see great potential that's a good sign. If it's not working like you thought it would in your head that's when you iterate or try a different direction.

Or maybe I didn't get your problem correctly?

replies.author: YesterdayOptimal3552
replies.body: oh it seems good of course; to my preference, I have just been doing things one by one without prototyping.

replies.author: josh_the_dev
replies.body:
Yes prototyping is good to verify your ideas are actually working out before committing to month of your time to a project that is flawed at its core. Prototype doesn't have to be pretty, no polish, only the minimal version that answers a question. Usually something like "is [my main mechanic] actually fun even without all the story, graphics and other less important features".
Obviously depends on your game idea a bit

replies.author: YesterdayOptimal3552
replies.body: I got it, small tests to avoid a big failure. thanks

comments.author: ponderdiggums
comments.body:
Write your Game Design Document. Look these up if you've never made one before. Be very thorough, use references, define your pillars and goals, platform, engine, controls and gameplay, art pipeline, etc.   
  
Go through it with Claude and plan - I use my own kanban board and use some agile concepts to keep the flow going as planned. I separate into milestones that are broken up into sprints, and go over what we expect at the end of each week (which should sort of line up with my usage limits and resets).  
  
Once the plan is clear, have Claude begin developing. As tasks move down the board, you test them and weigh in and iterate with claude until you're satisfied. I'm comfortable with Unity and Unreal so I do a lot of iterating by hand alongside claude. Additionally, I had it build a tool for Unity and Unreal that lets me annotate what I'm seeing (both picture and video format) and ties this to timestamps, build # and whatever assets are involved, then feeds a slice with all of my annotations from the last session to claude with a skill - this helps testing and troubleshooting a TON. 

For art, sfx and music I can make my own - I'll also grab some pieces for a mood board, and this will develop a style guide to start from. I'll use Astra to quickly iterate out additional poses and angles and such. That's the concept art. Then I make some of the models in Blender or Aesprite or whatever (depending on what sort of game I'm making). I go back to Astra again, and use the concept art, style guide and models I've built to get the art and animation pipeline going. For music, Suno does okay - again I make my own stuff and then expand on it from there. SFX I might just do myself or use some free stuff online (make sure its free).

It's working really well for me. FWIW I've worked in games and software for a while, and doing the same sort of stuff as a hobby long before that too. Artist, Design, Writing/Worldbuilding, QA, Prod - you name it. Knowing how these different disciplines all come together to spit out a game is advantageous here, so I've been pretty fortunate.

replies.author: YesterdayOptimal3552
replies.body: so careful planning is the key?

replies.author: ponderdiggums
replies.body: That's one yeah, I'd say the other key is actively iterating with meaningful feedback - you want to be clear with what's missing or not landing. IE "this looks bad" is usually a waste of tokens vs "the blending state between run and idle anims stutters when these units are mounted, but does not repro for either unit when unmounted", sometimes you need to sit down and draw a diagram in MSpaint, sometimes you need screenshots from multiple angles to help identify what's wrong, etc. And of course, general game development knowledge from different disciplines is helpful in identifying issues, knowing the verbiage and flow, managing expectations and so on.

comments.author: KnownPride
comments.body:
If I can imagine clearly what I want to draw/write/compose and how to do it, then it will be faster to make it myself than to elaborate/give context to AI.

mmm.. no.... hell no..

I know what i want to make, do  it myself took like days, use ai 5min + half a hour polishing.

replies.author: YesterdayOptimal3552
replies.body: it is ok if you're ok. for me, it seems they are not so different when I want to decide myself at the "every single pixel" or "every single letter" level. On the broader/quicker level, of course, ai should be more convenient.
